newsitem.title: USA: Suffolk County, N.Y., consultants blast LIPA plan.
newsitem.headline: Suffolk County, N.Y., consultants blast LIPA plan.

text.p: Consultants hired by the Suffolk County legislature in New York State to review Gov George Pataki's plan to partly takeover the Long Island Lighting Co on Tuesday rejected many of its claims.

Michael Caracciolo, a Republican who chairs the legislature's energy and environment committee, said it plans to hold public hearings over the next three to four weeks, but declined to predict what action it might take after that.

He added that contrary to what LILCO has said, the consultants found there was no need to move swiftly to avoid the risk that new federal tax rules will derail the deal by imposing capital gains taxes.

"Oh, there's plenty of time. There are really two key approvals this deal hinges on," he said, referring to a decision by the state Public Authorities Control Board, which must approve bond sales by state agencies, and the Internal Revenue Service, which was expected to publish new rules governing how such transactions would be taxed.

"The IRS, based on this information in the industry, that is not going to happen. The earliest would be the fall, and it might actually drag it out until winter and beyond," Caracciolo said, referring to one of the consultants.

A spokesman for the Long Island Power Authority (LIPA), the state agency that would partly takeover LILCO by buying assets from it and Brooklyn Union Gas, was not immediately available to comment. The two companies plan to merge. The Republican governor, in prepared remarks, again stressed the potential savings for Long Island ratepayers, who now pay some of the highest electricity prices in the nation.

The study, done by a Maryland attorney, Scott Hempling, and a Massachusetts-based special consultant, Richard LaCapra, found the deal, which calls for LIPA to sell almost $7.3 billion of tax-exempt debt, would only produce half of the projected savings, saying they only added up to about $9 for each customer each month.

Instead, it recommended that LIPA buy LILCO's total electric assets, sell the competitive ones, like power plants, and give the ratepayers, who financed them, the proceeds. A manager should be selected to run the assets that would be used to maintain monopoly services, like local power lines.
"There is no "worst-case scenario" worse than the LIPA proposal," the study said, according to a summary released by the Suffolk County legislature.
